## What this post is, and is not
This is a **method**, written for PhD students and team members joining the
semi-arid work. None of it is in `plant` yet; the pin above is the state of
`develop` it was written against. The figures come from a deliberately small toy
model in base R, not from `plant`, so you can read every line of it. The toy has
no competition and one made-up plant. It is there to make the ideas visible, not
to predict anything.
:::

## The question

We want to use `plant` and
[`regnans`](https://github.com/traitecoevo/regnans) to ask eco-evolutionary
questions about semi-arid Australia. Which combinations of traits are
evolutionarily stable under a given rainfall regime? Can annual herbs, perennial
grasses and woody shrubs coexist, and on what terms? How does the answer change
between an upslope patch that sheds water and a downslope patch that receives it?

Every one of those questions runs through one calculation: the
[invasion fitness](../../glossary.qmd#invasion-fitness) of a rare
[mutant](../../glossary.qmd#mutant) strategy in the environment created by the
[residents](../../glossary.qmd#resident). Get that number, and the
[community assembly](../../glossary.qmd#community-assembly) machinery in `regnans`
does the rest. The difficulty is that the way `plant` computes it today was built
for forests.

## How plant calculates fitness now

In a forest, a patch is reset by disturbance and then develops along the same
trajectory every time. So a patch's age since disturbance tells you everything
about it: how tall the canopy is, how much light reaches the ground, how much
competition a seedling faces. Disturbance strikes patches independently, so
across the landscape the [distribution of patch
ages](../../glossary.qmd#patch-age-distribution) $P(a)$ stays fixed even though
every patch is changing.

That makes fitness cheap. A mutant seed that lands in a patch of age $a$ goes on
to produce some number of dispersing seeds over its life, $\tilde R(a)$. Its
fitness is the average of that over all the ages it might land in
[@Falster-2017; @Falster-2015]:

$$
R = \int_0^\infty P(a)\, \tilde R(a)\, \mathrm{d}a .
$$

Above one, the mutant can invade. To compute it, `plant` runs **one** patch from
bare ground, introduces mutant [nodes](../../glossary.qmd#node) along the way, and
weights each by how common patches of its age are. One run stands in for the whole
landscape. The [Theory page](../../theory/adaptive-dynamics.qmd#sec-invasion-fitness)
has the details.

## What breaks in the semi-arid

Three things that made the forest calculation work are gone.

- **There is no reset.** Without stand-replacing disturbance, nothing pins a patch
  to a known starting point, so patch age tells you nothing.
- **The environment has memory.** Rain arrives as pulses of random size at random
  times. The soil stores them, and plants store carbon and grow roots in response.
  What a seedling meets depends on the recent sequence of rain, not on a single
  number.
- **Rain is shared.** A big wet year is wet across a whole catchment. Patches are
  not independent draws, so the landscape does not average itself out at every
  moment the way a disturbance mosaic does.

And a fourth thing is added: landscape position. An upslope patch and a
downslope patch receive different effective rainfall from the same storms.

The obvious response is brute force: simulate many patches under many random
draws of rainfall and count seeds. That is expensive, and it turns out to be
unnecessary.

## The principle underneath

The forest calculation is one application of a more general result. Metz and
Gyllenberg showed that in a metapopulation of patches, a rare mutant's fitness is
its expected lifetime output of dispersing seeds, averaged over the [**stationary
distribution**](../../glossary.qmd#stationary-distribution) of the local states
that its seeds land in
[@Metz-2001; @Gyllenberg-2001].

"Stationary" means the long-run distribution: the fraction of time, or of
patches, in each state once the system has settled down. In a forest the local
state that matters is patch age, and its stationary distribution is $P(a)$. That
is the only reason patch age appears in the formula. The principle does not care
what the state is.

In the semi-arid, the local state is the soil-water profile together with the
plants standing in it. So the job becomes: find the stationary distribution of
soil-water states, and find the lifetime output of a seed that lands in each.

## Westoby's suggestion: the distribution of soil-water states

Mark Westoby suggested starting exactly there: work out the distribution of
soil-water states that a rainfall regime and a landscape position produce, then
ask what each growth form makes of it. The idea goes back to his 1980 paper, which
described a climate not by its mean aridity but by the probability distribution of
"types of time": just wetted, staying wet, and drying out
[@Westoby-1980]. Different growth forms use different types of time, and each
distribution should have a characteristic mixture of growth forms. He did not
compute that mixture for any climate. Mark describes the idea as loosely like
coexistence by subdividing successional time in a forest, except that rainfall
pulses, not disturbance, create the different kinds of time. That is why the
forest calculation is the right place to start.

The first half is now easy. Under pulsed rain, with random timing and depth, and
losses that depend on how wet the soil is, the long-run distribution of soil
moisture has a closed form [@RodriguezIturbe-1999; @Laio-2001]. In the simplest
version, storms arrive at rate $\lambda$ with mean depth $\alpha$ and the soil
loses a fixed fraction $k$ of its water per day; the stationary soil water is then
gamma-distributed with shape $\lambda / k$ and scale $\alpha$.

```{r}
#| label: toy-model
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The toy model: rain, a soil bucket, and one plant"
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
set.seed(1)

## Rain: storms at random times, exponential depths. Soil: a bucket losing a
## fixed fraction k of its water per day. Simulated exactly, sampled daily.
years  <- 10000
lambda <- 1 / 15   # storms per day
alpha  <- 12       # mean storm depth, mm
k      <- 1 / 25   # fraction of soil water lost per day
ndays  <- years * 365
n_ev   <- rpois(1, lambda * ndays)
t_ev   <- sort(runif(n_ev, 0, ndays))
d_ev   <- rexp(n_ev, 1 / alpha)
day    <- ceiling(t_ev)
inc    <- numeric(ndays)
agg    <- tapply(d_ev * exp(-k * (day - t_ev)), day, sum)
inc[as.integer(names(agg))] <- agg
x <- numeric(ndays); x[1] <- inc[1]
for (i in 2:ndays) x[i] <- x[i - 1] * exp(-k) + inc[i]
rain <- inc
burn <- 3650                               # let the bucket forget its start
x <- x[-(1:burn)]; rain <- rain[-(1:burn)]
nd <- length(x)

## One plant. A seedling starting on day t0 dies in any dry spell where soil
## water stays below theta_d for D days in a row. From age m it makes seed at a
## rate set by soil water above theta_c. It lives at most L days. Returns
## lifetime output by start day, and zero on days too dry to germinate.
lifetime_output <- function(x, theta_g = 25, theta_d = 8, D = 90,
                            m = 3 * 365, L = 40 * 365, theta_c = 10) {
  nd  <- length(x)
  run <- integer(nd); r <- 0L
  for (i in seq_len(nd)) { r <- if (x[i] < theta_d) r + 1L else 0L; run[i] <- r }
  nk <- rep(.Machine$integer.max, nd)
  nk[run == D] <- which(run == D)
  nk <- rev(cummin(rev(nk)))                  # next killing day at or after t
  C  <- c(0, cumsum(pmax(x - theta_c, 0)))
  t0 <- seq_len(nd)
  start <- t0 + m
  end   <- pmin(nk - 1L, t0 + L, nd)
  out <- ifelse(end >= start, C[end + 1] - C[start], 0)
  out[x <= theta_g] <- 0                      # did not germinate
  out[t0 + L > nd]  <- NA                     # life would run past the end
  out
}

## Seeds wait in the soil until rain wets it past theta_g, so every life starts
## on a germinating rain: a day the soil crosses theta_g on the way up.
germinating_rains <- function(x, theta_g = 25) {
  which(x[-1] > theta_g & x[-length(x)] <= theta_g) + 1L
}

## Strategy A, and strategy B: survives 95-day dry spells, but needs more water
## before it seeds. Keep the rains whose cohorts can live out their lives, and
## scale output so A exactly replaces itself (R = 1), as a resident would.
RA <- lifetime_output(x)
RB <- lifetime_output(x, D = 95, theta_c = 10.2)
ev <- germinating_rains(x)
ev <- ev[!is.na(RA[ev]) & !is.na(RB[ev])]
c_scale <- 1 / mean(RA[ev])
RA <- RA * c_scale
RB <- RB * c_scale

green <- "#2E6B3F"; sand <- "#C08A3E"; grey <- "grey55"
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
            theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank()))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-soil
#| fig-cap: "**One long run samples the distribution.** (a) Three years of the toy: storms (bars) and the soil water they leave behind (line). (b) Soil water over all 10,000 years of the run (histogram) against the closed-form stationary distribution (line). They agree because the run is stationary: averaging over time is averaging over the distribution."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.4
idx <- 1:(3 * 365)
pa <- ggplot(data.frame(t = idx / 365, x = x[idx], rain = rain[idx])) +
  geom_col(aes(t, rain), fill = grey, width = 1 / 365) +
  geom_line(aes(t, x), colour = green, linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "years", y = "mm", title = "(a) storms and soil water")
pb <- ggplot(data.frame(x = x), aes(x)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 80, fill = "grey80") +
  stat_function(fun = dgamma, args = list(shape = lambda / k, scale = alpha),
                colour = green, linewidth = 0.8) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 90)) +
  labs(x = "soil water (mm)", y = "density",
       title = "(b) time spent in each state")
pa + pb + plot_layout(widths = c(1.6, 1))
```

So for any rainfall regime and landscape position, we can write down the
distribution of soil-water states without simulating anything. That is a fast
screen: for anything that depends only on the water state *at the moment*, such
as carbon gain at a given leaf area, the long-run average is just an average over
this curve. It is also a check. Whatever we simulate must reproduce the curve, or
the run has not settled.

## Why the distribution alone is not fitness

The trouble is that a plant's lifetime output depends on the **order** in which
states arrive, not only on how often each occurs. Drought kills by duration: a
long run of dry days, not one dry day. Establishment needs a wet start followed by
enough wet weeks.

First, when does a plant's life start? As Mark Westoby pointed out to us, seeds
are shed at one time and germinate at another. Buried seeds wait in the soil,
dying at a roughly steady rate, until a rain wets it enough to germinate them. A
seed shed on a dry day is not lost, only waiting, so every life starts on a
germinating rain. In the toy that is a rain that takes the soil past 25 mm,
which happens about
`r sprintf("%.0f", length(germinating_rains(x)) / (nd / 365))` times a year.
@fig-arrival shows the lifetime output of the cohort each of those rains starts.

```{r}
#| label: fig-arrival
#| fig-cap: "**Lifetime output depends on what follows germination.** Each point is the lifetime seed output of one toy cohort, by the day the rain that germinated it fell, over 60 years. Every cohort starts from much the same soil, just wetted past the germination threshold. Some germinate just before a long drought and die young; others germinate after one and live for decades. Grey lines mark the day each lethal drought reaches 90 days and kills every plant then alive."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3
win <- 1:(60 * 365)
dry <- rle(x < 8)
dry_end <- cumsum(dry$lengths)
dry_start <- dry_end - dry$lengths + 1
kill_days <- dry_start[dry$values & dry$lengths >= 90] + 89
kill_days <- kill_days[kill_days %in% win]
ev60 <- ev[ev %in% win]
ggplot(data.frame(t = ev60 / 365, R = RA[ev60])) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = kill_days / 365, colour = "grey85") +
  geom_point(aes(t, R), size = 0.9, colour = green) +
  labs(x = "germination day (years)", y = "lifetime output")
```

The cleanest way to see it is to keep the distribution and destroy the order.
Shuffling the days of the soil-water record leaves the histogram exactly as it
was, but long dry spells vanish, because dry days no longer come in runs.

```{r}
#| label: fig-shuffle
#| fig-cap: "**Same distribution, different order, different fitness.** (a) The soil-water record and a shuffled copy of it have identical distributions; the two histograms overlap exactly. (b) The fitness of the same toy plant on each. On the real sequence it exactly replaces itself. On the shuffled one, with no long droughts, its fitness is about four times higher."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.2
xs <- sample(x)
RS <- lifetime_output(xs) * c_scale
es <- germinating_rains(xs)
es <- es[!is.na(RS[es])]
fit <- data.frame(series = c("real order", "shuffled"),
                  R = c(mean(RA[ev]), mean(RS[es])))
pa <- ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x, y = after_stat(density)), data.frame(x = x),
                 bins = 80, fill = green, alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_freqpoly(aes(x, y = after_stat(density)), data.frame(x = xs),
                bins = 80, colour = sand, linewidth = 0.8) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 90)) +
  labs(x = "soil water (mm)", y = "density", title = "(a) the distribution",
       subtitle = "filled: real order    line: shuffled")
pb <- ggplot(fit, aes(series, R, fill = series)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(green, sand)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "fitness R", title = "(b) the fitness")
pa + pb + plot_layout(widths = c(1.6, 1))
```

On the shuffled record the toy plant's fitness is
`r sprintf("%.1f", fit$R[2])`; on the real one it is 1. A fitness calculated from
the distribution alone cannot tell these two apart. So the distribution supplies
the **weights**, but something has to supply the **sequence** that follows each
starting state.

## The method: one long run, many germinating rains

Here is the cut-through. It is the forest calculation with time in place of
patch age.

1. **Run one patch for a long time** under one realisation of the rainfall
   process, with the resident community in it, until it settles into a steady
   state. Steady here means stationary: the community keeps fluctuating with the
   rain, but its long-run statistics stop changing. This burn-in is paid once.
   Save the state at the end of it.
2. **Introduce mutant seedlings at each germinating rain** in a window that
   starts after the burn-in. `plant` already introduces nodes at a schedule of
   times; only the schedule and the weighting change.
3. **Record each one's lifetime output** $\tilde R(t_i)$, running past the end of
   the window long enough for late arrivals to live out their lives.
4. **Average over the $N$ germinating rains** $t_1, \dots, t_N$ in the window:
$$
R = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde R(t_i) .
$$

Because the run is stationary, the germinating rains in the window are a fair
sample of all the germinating rains the climate produces, and the soil and stand
at those moments are a fair sample of the states that seedlings start from. So
averaging over them *is* the average over the stationary distribution of states
that seeds land in, which is what Metz and Gyllenberg ask for. And each cohort
carries the real sequence that follows it, which is what @fig-shuffle shows we
need. One run delivers both the weights and the sequence.

In code this is a small change. In the forest the weight on a seed arriving at
age $a$ is the patch-age density $P(a)$. Here the weight sits on the germinating
rains in the window, equally on each, and is zero everywhere else. Weighting
each rain equally assumes, as a first approximation, that when a seed was shed
does not matter, only that it survives in the soil until a rain germinates it.
Everything downstream, from the fitness integral in `plant` to the assembly loop
in `regnans`, is untouched.

## Annuals and perennials on the same run

For a long-lived shrub, one life spans dozens of rain pulses and several
droughts, so each individual experiences something close to the long-run average
and $R$ above is the right fitness. For an annual it is not. An annual lives one
season, and its population multiplies by a different factor every year: large
after a good year, near zero after a bad one. What matters then is the [**long-run growth
rate**](../../glossary.qmd#long-run-growth-rate), the average of the *logarithm*
of the yearly multiplication, not
the average multiplication itself [@Tuljapurkar-1980; @Metz-1992]. With a seed
bank that survives a year with probability $s$, a fraction $g$ of seeds
germinating, and $Y_t$ seeds per germinant in year $t$, an annual invades when

$$
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=1}^{N} \log\bigl(s\,(1-g) + g\,Y_t\bigr) > 0 .
$$

This is Cohen's classic germination problem [@Cohen-1966], and it is the
storage effect of coexistence theory [@Chesson-2000] computed directly instead
of decomposed into parts. The useful thing is that $Y_t$ comes from **the same
run**: introduce an annual node at each year's germinating rain, harvest it at the
end of the season. Annuals and perennials are judged on one run and one rainfall
series, which is what the annual–woody coexistence question needs. For in-between
life histories, like a perennial grass living ten years, the toy and the pilot will
tell us whether $R$ is close enough or the growth rate is needed.

## Uphill and downhill

Landscape position adds a dimension but not a new idea. Run one long patch per
position, both under the same storms. The upslope patch keeps each storm only up
to what its soil can hold and sheds the rest; the downslope patch receives that
excess on top of its own rain. Water only flows downhill, so the upslope run can
go first and hand its runoff, storm by storm, to the downslope run. Because the
downslope gain comes in the same storms as the upslope loss, the two positions
must share one rain series. Then ask where seeds go. If a
seed produced in position $i$ lands in position $j$ with probability $D_{ij}$,
the expected number of offspring in $j$ per seed in $i$ is $D_{ij} \tilde R_j$.
With two positions that is a $2 \times 2$ matrix, and the mutant's fitness is its
largest eigenvalue: the long-run multiplication of a lineage that keeps moving
between positions. This is the same Metz and Gyllenberg result, now with two
kinds of patch [@Metz-2001]. It is also where source–sink structure appears: a
position where a strategy cannot replace itself can still hold it, fed by seed
from a position where it can.

## How long a run?

A fitness estimated from a finite window is noisy, because a few droughts more or
less in the window shift it. The question is how long the window must be, and the
toy gives a feel for the answer.

```{r}
#| label: fig-window
#| fig-cap: "**Comparisons converge faster than levels, if they share a rain series.** Spread (standard deviation) of toy fitness estimates against window length, across non-overlapping windows of the 10,000-year run. Green: the fitness of one strategy. Brown, solid: the difference in fitness between strategies A and B, estimated on the same rain series. Brown, dashed: the same difference estimated on separate series. The dotted line is the true difference; a comparison is resolved roughly where its curve falls well below it."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.6
yr <- (ev - 1) %/% 365                        # year of each germinating rain
W <- c(25, 50, 100, 200, 400)
spread <- do.call(rbind, lapply(W, function(wy) {
  block <- yr %/% wy
  keep  <- block < max(block)                 # drop the last, partial block
  mA <- tapply(RA[ev][keep], block[keep], mean)
  mB <- tapply(RB[ev][keep], block[keep], mean)
  nb <- length(mA)
  data.frame(
    years = wy,
    what  = c("fitness of A", "A vs B, same series", "A vs B, separate series"),
    sd    = c(sd(mA), sd(mB - mA), sd(mB[-1] - mA[-nb])))  # separate: next block
}))
true_diff <- mean(RB[ev] - RA[ev])
spread$what <- factor(spread$what, levels = c(
  "fitness of A", "A vs B, separate series", "A vs B, same series"))
ggplot(spread, aes(years, sd, colour = what, linetype = what)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) + geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = true_diff, linetype = 3, colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = 25, y = true_diff, label = "true A–B difference",
           hjust = 0, vjust = -0.5, size = 3.2, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = W) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(green, sand, sand)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(1, 2, 1)) +
  labs(x = "window length (years)", y = "spread of estimate",
       colour = NULL, linetype = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: window-numbers
#| include: false
lev   <- spread$sd[spread$what == "fitness of A"]
crn   <- spread$sd[spread$what == "A vs B, same series"]
ind   <- spread$sd[spread$what == "A vs B, separate series"]
## Variance scales as 1/window, so the run length needed for a given
## precision scales as variance: the saving from a shared series is (ind/crn)^2.
saving <- (ind / crn)^2
## Years for a 1% spread in a level, extrapolating variance ~ 1/window.
years_1pct <- max(W) * (lev[W == max(W)] / 0.01)^2
## Share of the spread in lifetime output explained by soil water at
## germination, grouped into deciles.
xg <- x[ev]
state_r2 <- summary(lm(RA[ev] ~ cut(xg, quantile(xg, 0:10 / 10),
                                    include.lowest = TRUE)))$r.squared
```

Three lessons, all from the toy, so read them as orders of magnitude rather than
numbers for TF24.

- **Levels are expensive.** The spread of one strategy's fitness is still
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * lev[W == max(W)])` after `r max(W)` years. Pinning
  fitness down to a percent by brute force would take something like
  `r formatC(signif(years_1pct, 1), format = "d", big.mark = ",")` years. The
  reason is that cohorts germinating within one lifetime of each other share the
  same future droughts, so their outputs rise and fall together; the run has to
  cover many lifetimes' worth of drought history before the luck averages out.
- **Comparisons are cheaper, if they share the rain.** Evolution acts on
  *differences* between strategies, and selection gradients are differences too.
  Running both strategies through the same rain series removes the luck of the
  draw that they have in common. In the toy, the same precision needs between
  `r sprintf("%.0f", min(saving))` and `r sprintf("%.0f", max(saving))` times
  fewer years, more as the window lengthens. After `r max(W)` years on a shared
  series, the difference between A and B, `r sprintf("%.2f", true_diff)`, is
  `r sprintf("%.1f", true_diff / crn[W == max(W)])` times its spread; on separate
  series the spread is still `r sprintf("%.1f", ind[W == max(W)] / true_diff)`
  times larger than the difference. The rule that
  follows is simple: **every fitness evaluation in an assembly uses the same rain
  series**, and we check the answer on a second series separately.
- **Sampling arrivals by soil-water state does not help.** Every cohort starts
  on a germinating rain, from much the same soil, and in the toy the soil water
  at germination explains `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * state_r2)` of the spread in
  lifetime output. The spread in @fig-arrival comes from what happens *after*
  germination, so choosing arrivals by their soil state cannot shorten the run.

There is one more route, which shortens each run rather than the total: give up
the single long run after the burn-in. The saved steady state is a library of
starting points: start many short mutant runs, each one lifetime long, from
states sampled along it. The total simulated time is similar, but each run is
short, they run in parallel, and gradients only need to be carried back through
one lifetime.

## What has to be built

`plant` cannot do this yet. It runs a patch for a fixed period after a
disturbance, from a fixed schedule of node introductions. The method needs a
**continuous patch**: one that keeps introducing nodes as it goes, can start from
a saved state, stops on a convergence test for the burn-in and a fixed horizon
for the window, keeps the lifetime output of every node while thinning the rest
of its history, and stops tracking old plants individually without losing their
seed output. That is [plant#519](https://github.com/traitecoevo/plant/issues/519),
and its requirements are listed there. It depends on rainfall arriving as
discrete events ([plant#628](https://github.com/traitecoevo/plant/issues/628)).
Handing runoff downhill one storm at a time needs only those events and a record
of each storm's runoff; patches that exchange water both ways need the
multi-patch work in [plant#427](https://github.com/traitecoevo/plant/issues/427).

Two things are open and will be answered by measurement, not argument. Does a
stand of mulga under pulsed rain settle into a steady state with no disturbance,
and how long does it take? And how long a window does a selection gradient need
for TF24, as opposed to the toy?

## Take-aways

- `plant`'s fitness was never really about patch age. It is an average of a
  seed's lifetime output over the stationary distribution of the states seeds land
  in; patch age is that state in a forest.
- In the semi-arid the state is soil water and the plants in it. Its distribution
  is known in closed form for a rainfall regime and landscape position, which gives
  a fast screen and a check.
- The distribution alone is not fitness, because drought and establishment depend
  on the sequence. Shuffling the toy's soil-water record leaves the distribution
  unchanged and roughly quadruples its fitness.
- One long stationary run, with mutant seedlings introduced at each germinating
  rain in a window, samples the states seedlings start from and keeps the
  sequence that follows each. In code it is a change of weights.
- Perennials use the average lifetime output; annuals use the average log of
  yearly multiplication; both come from the same run. Landscape positions combine
  through a small matrix.
- Fitness levels are very expensive to pin down; fitness differences on a shared
  rain series are many times cheaper. Always compare strategies on the same
  series.
